title: Given accounts where each is a name followed by emails, merge accounts that share any email. Return merged accounts with the name and sorted unique emails.
shortTitle: Accounts Merge — union emails that belong to the same person

s1_definition.profdef: Assign each distinct email an integer id, union all emails within the same account row, then group emails by their Union-Find root. Each root becomes one merged account; attach the owner name (recorded per email) and output the emails sorted. Two accounts merge transitively whenever they share at least one email.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India sometimes has the same customer registered under multiple profiles that share an email. If profile A and profile B share one email, they are the same person; and if B and C share another, then A, B, and C are all one person. You link shared emails, then gather every email that ends up under the same head into one clean profile.
s1_definition.oneliner: Union emails that appear together, then group by root — each root is one merged person with sorted emails.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Assign each distinct email an integer id, union all emails within the same account row, then group emails by their Union-Find root. Each root becomes one merged account; attach the owner name (recorded per email) and output the emails sorted. Two accounts merge transitively whenever they share at least one email.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India sometimes has the same customer registered under multiple profiles that share an email. If profile A and profile B share one email, they are the same person; and if B and C share another, then A, B, and C are all one person. You link shared emails, then gather every email that ends up under the same head into one clean profile.

**One line to remember:** Union emails that appear together, then group by root — each root is one merged person with sorted emails.

sections.s2_technical:
Give each first-seen email a unique id and remember which name owns it. For example: `emailToId.putIfAbsent(email, emailToId.size());` and `emailToName.put(email, name);`.

Within each account, union the first email's id with every other email's id, so all emails of one row share a root. For example: `union(id(firstEmail), id(otherEmail));`.

Group emails by their root into lists, sort each list, and prepend the owning name. For example: `root -> [name, sortedEmail1, sortedEmail2, ...]`. The time is dominated by sorting the emails, roughly n log n in the number of emails, with the unions being near-constant.

A senior nuance is that emails, not names, are the identity key, because two different people can share a name but never a verified email, so unioning on names would be incorrect.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a customer may appear as several profiles that must be merged into one golden record. Two profiles are the same customer if they share any verified email, and this merging is transitive. This is exactly how Accounts Merge works.

Problem 2 — The merged record must list every associated email once, in sorted order, under the customer's name. This is exactly the grouping-by-root-then-sort step.

The mini-project builds a `CustomerProfileMerger`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input has three profile rows for two people.

Step 1: Each distinct email gets an id and remembers its owner name.

Step 2: Within the first Rajesh row, the two emails are unioned; within the second Rajesh row, its emails are unioned, and because "raj@nbi.in" is shared, all three Rajesh emails end up with one root.

Step 3: Priya's single email forms its own root.

Step 4: Grouping by root yields two groups; each group's emails are sorted and the owner name is prepended.

Step 5: The output is one merged Rajesh profile with three sorted emails and one Priya profile.

```text

2026-10-26T23:35:00Z [INFO] Merged into 2 golden profiles
2026-10-26T23:35:00Z [INFO] Profile: [Rajesh, raj@nbi.in, rajesh.kumar@nbi.in, rajesh@nbi.in]
2026-10-26T23:35:00Z [INFO] Profile: [Priya, priya@nbi.in]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Accounts Merge is a Union-Find problem where the identity key is the email, not the name. I give every distinct email a unique integer id and record which name owns each email. Then, for each account row, I union the first email's id with every other email's id in that row, which makes all emails of a single profile share one root. Because unions are transitive, two profiles that each share an email with a third profile all collapse into one set.

To produce the output I group every email by its Union-Find root, sort the emails within each group, and prepend the owner's name. Sorting dominates the cost at roughly n log n in the number of emails, while the unions themselves are effectively constant.

In my project at National Bank of India's master data management, a single customer often appeared under several profiles that shared a verified email, and we needed one golden record per real person with all associated emails listed once in sorted order. Using the email as the merge key was critical, because two different customers can share a name but never a verified email, so unioning on names would have wrongly fused distinct people.
